Multiplicity is such an input and is undecided. S-001 requires totality over everything S-002 admits, and S-002 admits this body on its face.

ARITHMETIC VERIFIED (my own script, exact rationals; award@19=12, @21=11, @22=0, @23=0). A: sample level mean(19,22,23)=21.33->21, cycle-weighted pooled rate 16/3, restated 5.8182, 1500/5.8182 = 257.8125, S-014 reports 258. B: mean(22,23)=22.5 ties DOWN to 22, award@22=0, S-017's "award at the sample level not positive => restated rate zero", M is the sole admissible monster, S-013 stops, rungs=[], NOT FINITE. B is not a misreading: S-018's closing paragraph states explicitly that a PRESENT measurement restated to zero DOES reach the stop, "and halts the walk at a rung whose published award may be perfectly healthy."

WORSE THAN A TWO-WAY SPLIT — I found two further clause-legal readings. Freshest-entry (E1 alone): sample 19, ratio 1, rate 6.0, total 250. Kill-weighted pooling instead of cycle-weighted: rate 5.0741, restated 5.5354, total 271. S-017 declines kill-weighting for the LEVEL MEAN only; it says nothing about how two RATES combine. So "pooling" is a family, not a reading, and there are two independent axes of silence (which entries, and with what weight). Four legal answers: 250, 258, 271, NOT FINITE.

USER-IMPACT LENS — not a don't-care. Reading B reports level 20 UNREACHABLE for a character 100/1600 into level 19 that holds 540 recorded kills on a monster admissible and beatable at every rung. That is the "projection walled my character" bug class this project has filed repeatedly (L38 wall, L50 walls, grind livelocks); an operator watching the status pane sees the bot abandon combat progression on a mob it kills freely. Readings A/C/A' do the opposite harm — silently laundering a stale/corrupt aggregate into claimed reach, which is the exact failure the spec's own no-manufactured-reach principle exists to prevent. Both directions get filed. In-Sigma on three declared dimensions: 1 (value semantics), 2 (error taxonomy — OBSERVATION.md notes the consuming spec bands on precisely the reachable/unreachable distinction), and 12 (the first-segment monster the planner acts on).

HONEST TEMPER ON 5/5. The FULL reachable/unreachable flip needs the corrupt cell the witness names: a level-19 character cannot have produced its own cycles at levels 22-23, so E2 implies cross-character or cross-season contamination, not mere staleness. But the gap is not confined to that exhibit — with two entirely ordinary entries (all levels <= 19) the four readings still produce different restated rates and different rung costs, which moves S-011's winner where a second monster is close and therefore changes the monster handed to the executor. WHAT THE SPEC NEEDS: either an input precondition fixing at most one measurement per monster (which S-002 must then state, since the collection machinery is background and cannot be relied on to enforce it), or a selector clause that names which entry is THE measurement — plus, if the answer is pooling, the weight.

votes.reason:
Note first: no spec file path was given in my instructions (only clause IDs S-002/S-007/S-013 were cited), so I judged Σ-membership from the exhibited outputs alone, without opening anything on disk. That is sufficient for this lens, because the two outputs are fully stated.

A returns a one-rung plan — [(level 25, monster `cow`, cost 2340.0000)] — with a finite total cost of 2340. B returns an empty rung list and a total cost that is NOT FINITE. This is not a naming, labelling, field-ordering, structural, or formatting difference, and the rung list is not an unordered collection whose permutation is being compared: one output contains a rung and the other contains none, and the scalar the caller reads off the result differs between a finite number and no finite value at all. Any caller that asks "what does this cost?" or "is this reachable?" gets opposite answers.

That lands squarely on `value semantics`, a declared dimension of Σ. (If a consumer instead surfaces the non-finite total as an unreachable/error signal, the divergence merely relocates to `error taxonomy` — also in Σ — so it is observable under either reading; there is no reading on which A and B are the same behaviour described two ways.)

The mechanism behind it is coherent and squarely a spec silence rather than an artifact of the framing: with two catalogue rows both identifying `cow` and disagreeing on level (20 vs 13), the level-24 character sees a gap of 4 under row 1 (inside the paying band, 25 XP) and a gap of 11 under row 2 (zeroed by the published penalty). Because `cow` is the catalogue's only monster, first-row resolution yields a payer and last-row resolution yields no admissible earner at all, at which point the walk terminates with an empty plan. Uniqueness of catalogue rows per monster identity is exactly what neither S-002 nor S-007 asserts, and the catalogue RESIDUAL is described as handing off completeness, not consistency — so both resolutions satisfy the spec while producing different observable values.

SCOPE lens: this survives.

The artifact under test is the oracle itself — "ONE pure function ... Given a character state, a target character level, a body of learned observations, and the game's static catalogue." The catalogue is a declared ARGUMENT of the function under test (S-002, "Input domain"), not a collaborator the spec merely quotes as background. S-001 promises the oracle "returns for every input admitted by S-002", so if S-002 admits a catalogue carrying two rows naming `cow`, the oracle must produce an answer on it.

Literal test — if I implemented the oracle, could I even MAKE this choice? Yes, and I could not avoid it. Handed rows in which `cow` appears twice with conflicting level/hp, the oracle's own code decides which attributes feed S-007's published formula, S-009/S-010 candidacy, and S-011's ranking. No one else makes that call: the catalogue producer merely hands over rows; the beatability predicate is handed whatever monster the oracle already selected; the progression choice core consumes the finished result. The divergence (total 2340 vs. NOT FINITE via S-013) is entirely a difference in the oracle's return value on identical arguments.

The carve-outs do not cover it. "Explicitly NOT under test" names the progression choice core, the acquisition-cost pricer, the learning store's collection machinery, the beatability predicate, the planner/goal/arbiter, and skill choice. The catalogue is absent from that list and present on the argument list instead. The only catalogue-flavoured elision is the RESIDUAL "The monster catalogue's completeness", scoped by its own words to which monsters are present ("whether monsters that exist only transiently are in the catalogue"). Duplicate conflicting rows for a monster that IS present is a question of the catalogue's shape and the oracle's reading of it, not of membership; shedding completeness does not shed identity resolution, and a residual cannot be stretched past what it says.

This is also not a clausifier slip — S-002 and S-007 are load-bearing clauses about the oracle's own domain and its own computation, and the divergence is exhibited through them.

The only out-of-scope reading available is "the catalogue is upstream game data, so its well-formedness is the API's problem." That answers a different question (who should have prevented the input), not whose code diverges on it. The spec demonstrably knows how to shed a duty by naming it — the beatability predicate, S-020's loadout selection, S-008's collection machinery — and it never says the catalogue carries at most one row per identity, never declares duplicate rows inadmissible, and never delegates the resolution. The subject here, how the oracle resolves a repeated monster identity inside its own argument before pricing it, belongs to the artifact under test.

REAL. The quote is verbatim from S-007 (line 155) and is quoted in context: "Where the oracle must predict the XP a kill awards, it computes it from the game's published formula over the catalogue's attributes for that monster." That phrase presupposes a unique attribute set per monster but never establishes one, and prescribes nothing when a monster identity appears twice with conflicting attributes.

No clause settles it. S-002 admits "the static catalogue of monsters and their attributes" and constrains only the character state's fields and the target level — it imposes no keying, no uniqueness, no well-formedness condition on the catalogue. The RESIDUAL on the catalogue hands over COMPLETENESS only ("whether monsters that exist only transiently are in the catalogue... is the catalogue's concern"), which is membership, not consistency. S-011's tiebreak governs two distinct monsters that are exactly equal and forbids name-dependence; neither A nor B tie-breaks by name, and neither is choosing between two monsters. S-001's purity is satisfied by both — each is deterministic on identical arguments, including catalogue order.

Critically, nothing forbids B. B's path is entirely ordinary spec machinery: row 2 gives gap 11 >= 10, the published penalty zeroes the award, S-013's zero-reward stop fires, and S-012's reporting rule yields the rungs crossed (none) with a total that is NOT FINITE. That is a legal second reading, not a violation.

The arithmetic is sound and matches the spec's own worked example. S-021 (line 454) prices this exact character — level 24, 535-point bar, 462 damage — at 3.90000 Fights per kill. Row 1 gives gap 4, a non-zero penalty, award Round(20/24*20 + 200*0.04) = 25, rate 25/3.9, and 15000 / (25/3.9) = 2340 exactly, one rung to level 25.

This is a gap by the spec's own declared standard: it repeatedly legislates server-impossible inputs because "a total function must decide it" — S-019 decides progress at or beyond the requirement and progress below zero, S-017 decides recorded levels below one and above the maximum and even fixes tie-rounding direction so "no default may be allowed to choose it." A duplicated catalogue row is the same class of input and gets no such rule. The spec even leaves room for a third implementation that treats the two rows as two candidates for S-011 to rank, which further confirms the resolution is undetermined.

Minor caveat that does not change the verdict: the domain facts state the penalty at three points and leave gaps 1-4 unstated, so the exact figure 2340 depends on reading gap 4 as 100%. Any non-zero penalty still leaves A finite and B not finite, so the observable divergence stands.

The exhibit is arithmetically exact against the spec's own published example (S-021 itself states 3.90000 loop actions/kill for a level-24 character with a 535 bar taking 462 damage; row 1 awards 25 XP, row 2 awards 0, and 15000/(25/3.9) = 2340.0 exactly), so the divergence is not an artifact of the witness's numbers.

The spec genuinely fails to determine it, and does so in a way its own clauses make visible. S-011 ranks "the monsters admitted by S-009 and S-010" — read over rows that mandates row 1 (A), but S-011 ranks MONSTERS and there is exactly one monster, `cow`; the open question is what `cow`'s attributes ARE, which is upstream of any ranking S-011 performs. A catalogue loaded into a map keyed by monster code with last-write-wins — the most ordinary implementation there is — yields B and violates no sentence. Worse, the spec's two governing principles point opposite ways here: S-011's maximization selects the positive row, while S-017's ratified no-manufactured-reach principle ("an over-estimate manufactures reach and captures the decision, while an under-estimate only costs gear") favours the zero row. Neither S-002 nor S-007 states a key constraint, and the catalogue RESIDUAL hands off COMPLETENESS (transient monsters), not identity consistency, while S-001 demands totality over everything S-002 admits.

It fails the don't-care test decisively. A returns a finite 2340 with a crossed rung; B returns zero rungs and NOT FINITE, which under S-003 means the target was not reached at all. That is a reachability flip — the most consequential value this oracle emits, since the consuming progression core bands on it. B silently tells the bot that level 25 is unreachable by fighting and stalls combat progression on a monster the character can plainly beat; an operator watching that files a bug immediately. The two outcomes are in no sense equally acceptable.

The input is reachable by an ordinary route rather than only by file corruption: a cache holding two seasons of /monsters after a rebalance moved `cow` from level 13 to 20 produces exactly this duplicate-with-conflicting-attributes row.

Finally, the spec's own standard of care settles the question of whether it should have decided this. It explicitly decides progress below zero, recorded levels below one, levels above the game maximum, zero damage, and half-integer rounding ties — every one an input it states the server cannot produce, decided because (S-019) "a total function must decide it." Leaving a repeated monster identity undecided is inconsistent with that ratified discipline, and the repair is one sentence: declare at most one row per identity as a precondition on S-002, or state the resolution rule and which way it resolves. Severity is maximal as claimed (finite vs not-finite is a band change downstream), though likelihood is lower than 5/5 suggests.
